Chief
CHēF
adj. and n. (rendering Hebrew rō'sh, Greek prōtos and archē in compounds)
From Old French chief, from Latin caput, the head. The Hebrew rō'sh likewise means head and then, by the same natural extension, first, foremost, or principal. Greek forms the idea by compounding archē — whence archiereus, chief priest; architektōn, master builder; and, in a phrase found nowhere in Greek literature before Peter used it, archipoimēn, chief Shepherd.

Biblical Definition

Chief in Scripture is a word about rank, and the New Testament takes hold of it in order to turn it inside out. The Lord Jesus does not deny that there is a chief place; He redefines the road to it: “And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant” (Mat 20:27). The ambition is not forbidden but redirected, and the redirection is total, since the way up is the way down and the currency of greatness is service. Paul then applies the word to himself in the one category no man competes for: “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1Ti 1:15) — written not in his unconverted days but as an apostle, in the present tense, so that the chiefest of the apostles reckons himself chiefest of sinners and finds the two entirely compatible. The word marks out Christ Himself in two great titles. He is the foundation stone that governs the whole structure: “Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20); and He is the Shepherd over every under-shepherd, whose appearing is the day of reckoning and reward: “And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away” (1Pe 5:4). Chief is finally used of what a man loves most, and the psalmist in exile makes his own affections the test: if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth. Every man has a chief joy; the question is only what it is.

Webster 1828 Definition

Highest in rank, office, or importance; first or principal; and as a noun the head or leader of a body of men — whence chief priest, chief corner stone, chief Shepherd, and Paul's confession that he is chief of sinners.

expand to see more

CHIEF, adj. 1. Highest in office or rank; principal; as a chief priest, the chief butler.

2. Principal or most eminent in any quality or action; most distinguished; as the chief excellence of a work.

3. First in affection, or in the estimation of the mind; as, my chief joy. Psalm 137.

4. n. A commander; a leader; the person highest in authority over a body of men.

5. In Scripture, whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant. Matt. 20. The chief corner stone. Eph. 2. The chief Shepherd. 1 Pet. 5.

Key Scripture

Matthew 20:27 — "And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant:"

1 Timothy 1:15 — "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief."

Ephesians 2:20 — "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;"

1 Peter 5:4 — "And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away."

Modern Corruption

Servant language is annexed to leadership without altering it, so that the vocabulary of Matthew 20 decorates the same hierarchies of ambition and status it was given to overturn.

expand to see more

The command of Mat 20:27 has been so thoroughly absorbed into the language of modern leadership that it can now be quoted without cost. Servant terminology is applied to offices whose actual operation — the pursuit of platform, the guarding of position, the assessment of people by their usefulness — is untouched by it. The Lord's words were not a style of leading but a reversal of the thing itself: the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them; but it shall not be so among you. The mark of the reversal is concrete and unmistakable, since it appears where advantage is surrendered rather than where humility is expressed. He who washed feet and went to a cross set the standard, and He set it in actions no vocabulary can imitate.

The corruption has a mirror image in which the word chief is thought to be abolished altogether — as though Christ had taught that there is no rank, no office, and no authority in the church. He taught nothing of the kind. He appointed apostles, the New Testament names elders who rule and are worthy of double honour, and Peter, writing to elders, warns them against lording it over God's heritage while assuming they genuinely oversee the flock. Authority is real and is answerable, which is exactly why the chief Shepherd's appearing is set before them as both incentive and reckoning (1Pe 5:4). The principle to recover is that Scripture abolishes neither office nor ambition but reassigns them: office exists for the flock's good, and the only ambition it permits is to be spent.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rō'sh is head, top, or chief, whence first and principal. Greek expresses the idea by prōtos, first, and by compounds of archē — archiereus (chief priest), archipoimēn (chief Shepherd), akrogōniaios (chief corner stone).

expand to see more

Hebrew rō'sh (H7218) — head, top, chief, beginning; the head of a house, the top of a mountain, and the first of a series alike.

Greek prōtos (G4413) — first, foremost, chief; of whom I am chief (1Ti 1:15) and whosoever will be chief among you (Mat 20:27).

Greek archipoimēn (G750) — chief Shepherd; a compound found only at 1Pe 5:4, setting Christ over every under-shepherd.

Greek akrogōniaios (G204) — chief corner stone, the stone at the extreme angle governing the alignment of two walls (Eph 2:20).

Greek archiereus (G749) — chief priest or high priest; used both of the Aaronic office and, in Hebrews, of Christ's greater priesthood.

Usage

"Of the way to greatness: whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant (Mat 20:27)."

"Of Paul's estimate of himself: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief (1Ti 1:15)."

"Of Christ's titles: the chief corner stone (Eph 2:20); the chief Shepherd shall appear (1Pe 5:4)."
